title: “FAMILY FIRST” SOUNDS HOLY… UNTIL YOUR FAMILY TAKES THE PLACE OF GOD
paragraphs: “FAMILY FIRST” SOUNDS HOLY… UNTIL YOUR FAMILY TAKES THE PLACE OF GOD

What if the people you love most have quietly become the reason you keep saying no to Jesus? The uncomfortable truth about family, misplaced devotion, spiritual compromise, and the Savior who never asked you to stop loving your family—only to stop putting anyone above Him.
There is a sentence that sounds so beautiful, so responsible, so deeply Christian, that almost nobody thinks to question it.
“God knows my heart. My family comes first.”
And sometimes, those words come from a genuinely loving heart.
A father working overtime because his children need food.
A mother staying awake beside a sick child.
A husband caring for his exhausted wife.
A daughter sacrificing her own comfort to look after aging parents.
There is something sacred about such love. Scripture does not condemn it. In fact, God commands us to care for our households.
But there is another version of that sentence.
A version we rarely talk about.
The version spoken when obedience to Jesus becomes inconvenient.
When biblical truth threatens family traditions.
When a relative demands that we compromise our convictions.
When a parent uses love to control an adult child's conscience.
When a spouse pressures the other to abandon a clear biblical responsibility.
When family approval begins to matter more than God's approval.
And suddenly, a sentence that once expressed beautiful responsibility becomes something else entirely.
A respectable excuse.
A spiritual hiding place.
An altar we never intended to build.
Because there is a terrifying possibility that deserves our attention:
Some Christians are not putting family first under God. They are putting family in God's place.
And the difference can be almost invisible.
Until following Jesus costs them something.
Imagine a man sitting in his car outside his own house.
The engine is off. His hands are still gripping the steering wheel.
He has just come from a conversation that has shaken him.
He knows he needs to make something right. He needs to tell the truth, turn away from a sinful practice, and stop pretending that everything is fine.
But he knows what will happen when he walks through that door.
His family will be upset.
His wife may misunderstand.
His parents may accuse him of becoming too religious.
His relatives may laugh at him.
So he whispers something that sounds reasonable.
“Lord, You understand. I have to keep peace in my family.”
And perhaps the most frightening part is that he genuinely believes he is being faithful.
He does not hate Jesus.
He has not announced that he is leaving the faith.
He still attends church when he can. He still believes the Bible. He still prays when life becomes unbearable.
But when the desires of his family collide with the commands of Christ, he has already decided whose voice will win.
Not because he consciously rejected God.
But because somewhere along the way, keeping everyone happy became more important than obeying the One who saved him.
And before we judge that man, we should ask ourselves something.
How many times have we done exactly the same thing?
Jesus spoke directly into this tension, and His words are far more confronting than the comfortable Christianity many of us have learned to practice.
In Matthew 10:37, Jesus declares:
“He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me: and he that loveth son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.” (KJV)
Read that again.
He did not say that loving your parents is wrong.
He did not say that your children are unimportant.
He did not say that a husband should neglect his wife or that a mother should abandon her responsibilities.
He said something far more searching.
Whoever loves them MORE THAN ME.
In the Greek text, the expression is:
ὁ φιλῶν πατέρα ἢ μητέρα ὑπὲρ ἐμὲ
ho philōn patera ē mētera hyper eme
Meaning, in context, “the one who loves father or mother more than Me.”
The crucial expression is ὑπὲρ ἐμέ (hyper eme)—“more than Me.”
That is where the issue becomes painfully clear.
Jesus is not condemning family affection.
He is confronting misplaced supremacy.
The problem is not that you love your family deeply.
The problem begins when you love their approval more than His truth, their comfort more than His commands, or their acceptance more than your faithfulness to Him.
Because a good gift can become an idol when it occupies the place reserved for the Giver.
And family is one of God's most beautiful gifts.
Which is precisely why it can become one of our most difficult tests.
Nobody wakes up one morning and announces, “Today, I am going to make an idol out of my family.”
It happens quietly.
You stop confronting a destructive family pattern because you do not want conflict.
You remain silent about your faith because you fear being rejected.
You excuse dishonesty because a relative benefits from it.
You allow your children's activities to consume every part of life until prayer, worship, Scripture, and discipleship become whatever is left over.
You teach your children to pursue success, comfort, grades, careers, possessions, and reputation.
But they rarely see you seek first the kingdom of God.
And all the while, you tell yourself that everything you are doing is for your family.
But what if the greatest thing your family needs is not another sacrifice of your spiritual convictions?
What if they need to see someone who loves Jesus enough to obey Him even when obedience is costly?
Not loudly.
Not arrogantly.
Not with self-righteousness.
But faithfully.
Because children do not only learn what we say about God.
They watch what we surrender to Him.
They notice what makes us compromise.
They learn what we truly worship by observing what we are unwilling to lose.
And that thought should make every Christian parent examine their heart.
One day, your children may not remember every gift you bought them.
They may not remember every holiday you paid for.
They may not remember every sacrifice you made to give them a comfortable life.
But they may remember whether Jesus was truly Lord in your home.
Or merely Someone you talked about whenever it was convenient.
This is why the words of Joshua are so powerful.
In Joshua 24:15, he declares:
“But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.” (KJV)
Notice the order.
Joshua did not say, “As for me and my house, we will serve whatever keeps our household comfortable.”
He did not make family happiness the final authority.
He placed his household under the authority of the Lord.
The Hebrew expression is:
וַאֲנִי וּבֵיתִי נַעֲבֹד אֶת־יְהוָה
va'ani uveiti na'avod et-YHWH
“But as for me and my household, we will serve the LORD.”
The verb נַעֲבֹד (na'avod) means “we will serve,” carrying the sense of service or worship within this covenant declaration.
Joshua's statement was not a promise that his family would never struggle, never sin, or never disagree.
It was a declaration of allegiance.
And that is what a Christ-centered family needs.
Not the appearance of perfection.
But a clear understanding of whom the household ultimately serves.
Yet there is another passage that many Christians find difficult.
Luke 14:26 records Jesus saying:
“If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple.” (KJV)
At first glance, those words can feel shocking.
Did Jesus really command us to hate our families?
No—not in the ordinary sense of malicious hostility or contempt.
The Greek word used is μισεῖ (misei), from μισέω (miseō), commonly meaning “to hate.”
But language must be understood in its literary and biblical context.
Jesus uses a forceful contrast to communicate the incomparable priority of discipleship. Matthew 10:37 helps clarify that the issue is loving family more than Christ.
This kind of comparative expression also appears in the Old Testament, where Genesis 29:30–31 contrasts Jacob's love for Rachel and Leah.
The point is not that Christians should become cruel, unloving, or emotionally detached.
The point is that our loyalty to Jesus must be so supreme that every competing allegiance becomes secondary by comparison.
And Luke 14 does not stop with family relationships.
Jesus continues by speaking of carrying one's cross and counting the cost of discipleship.
He is not selling a comfortable religious lifestyle.
He is calling people to surrender.
A surrender that may cost reputation.
Approval.
Security.
Possessions.
And sometimes even the support of those closest to us.
But here is where we must be extraordinarily careful.
Because some people have used verses like these to justify behavior that directly contradicts the character and commands of Christ.
A father neglects his children and calls it ministry.
A husband abandons his responsibilities and calls it sacrifice.
A religious leader demands unquestioning loyalty and tells people that loving their families is evidence of weak faith.
Someone uses “God first” as permission to become harsh, controlling, emotionally absent, or financially irresponsible.
That is not what Jesus taught.
Putting God first never gives us permission to disobey God in the way we treat our families.
The same Jesus who demands supreme allegiance also commands love.
The same Savior who calls us to costly discipleship condemns religious excuses for neglecting parents.
In Mark 7:9–13, Jesus rebukes people who used religious traditions concerning offerings dedicated to God as a way of avoiding their responsibility to honor their father and mother.
Think about that.
Jesus Himself confronted the practice of using religion as an excuse to avoid family obligations.
And in 1 Timothy 5:8, Scripture warns that anyone who fails to provide for their own household has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
That is a serious warning.
Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Ephesians 6:4 instructs fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, but to raise them in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
And when Jesus was suffering on the cross, He still showed concern for His mother, entrusting her care to the beloved disciple in John 19:26–27.
Even in His agony, He did not treat love and responsibility as disposable.
So the biblical question is not whether family matters.
It absolutely does.
The question is whether we have allowed family to become an authority greater than the Lord who created it.
There is a profound difference between loving your family because you love God and disobeying God because you fear losing your family.
And some of us know exactly what that second sentence feels like.
Maybe you are the only serious believer in your household.
You love your parents, but they mock your commitment to Scripture.
You love your spouse, but following Jesus has introduced difficult conversations into your marriage.
You love your relatives, but certain family traditions require you to participate in something your conscience, informed by Scripture, cannot accept.
You want peace.
You want belonging.
You want to sit at the family table without feeling like the difficult one.
You do not want every gathering to become an argument.
And the thought of disappointing people who raised you, cared for you, and sacrificed for you feels unbearable.
Jesus understands that pain.
He does not ask you to enjoy conflict.
Romans 12:18 tells believers, as far as it depends on them, to live peaceably with everyone.
But peace is not the same as compromise.
You can be gentle without surrendering truth.
You can honor your parents without obeying sinful demands.
You can love your spouse without participating in wrongdoing.
You can respect family traditions without treating them as more authoritative than Scripture.
You can establish necessary boundaries without becoming cruel.
And you can remain faithful to Jesus without turning every disagreement into a battle.
Sometimes the most Christlike response is a quiet, trembling sentence:
“I love you. I always will. But I cannot disobey Jesus to make this easier.”
That sentence may hurt.
It may cost you approval.
It may bring tears that nobody else sees.
But obedience to Christ is not always accompanied by applause.
Sometimes it is accompanied by loneliness.
And sometimes the loneliness comes from the very people you hoped would understand you most.
Jesus warned His disciples that allegiance to Him could divide households. In Matthew 10:34–36, He spoke of the painful conflict His coming would sometimes produce, even among close relatives.
He was not commanding His followers to manufacture division.
He was telling them that faithfulness could provoke opposition.
That distinction matters.
Because the goal of Christian discipleship is not to win arguments against our families.
It is to remain faithful to Jesus while loving people truthfully.
And that brings us to something even more personal.
What if your greatest struggle is not a family member asking you to deny Jesus?
What if it is simply that your family has become the center of your identity?
You are terrified of your children failing because their achievements have become the measure of your worth.
You cannot accept a loved one's disagreement because their approval has become the foundation of your security.
You constantly try to control the future because you cannot bear the thought of losing what you love.
Your prayers have slowly become demands that God preserve the life you have designed.
You still believe in Him.
But you have begun treating Him as the protector of your personal kingdom rather than the Lord of your life.
And perhaps the deepest question is not whether you would die for your family.
You probably would.
The question is whether you are willing to trust your family to God.
Because love can become controlling when it refuses to surrender.
Protection can become fear when it forgets God's sovereignty.
And devotion can become idolatry when the thought of losing something becomes more powerful than our trust in the Lord.
This does not mean that grief, anxiety, or the fear of losing loved ones automatically proves idolatry. Jesus Himself wept at Lazarus's tomb.
Human love hurts when threatened.
The issue is not whether we experience pain.
The issue is where we turn with that pain, and whom we ultimately trust and obey.
Remember Abraham.
Genesis 22 describes one of Scripture's most difficult accounts: God's testing of Abraham concerning Isaac, the son of promise.
Abraham loved Isaac.
And God's promise concerning Abraham's descendants was bound up with this son.
Yet Abraham was called to trust the Lord even when he could not understand how the promise and the command could fit together.
At the decisive moment, God stopped Abraham, and a ram was provided.
The account does not authorize parents to harm children or claim that God is commanding them to do so. It is a unique biblical test within the history of God's covenant promises.
Its significance includes Abraham's faith, God's provision, and the truth that the Lord Himself is trustworthy.
And in the larger story of redemption, it points our attention toward something even more astonishing.
God did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all, as Romans 8:32 declares.
At Calvary, salvation did not come through a parent's willingness to sacrifice a child.
It came through the willing self-giving of Jesus Christ, the eternal Son, according to the Father's saving purpose.
And this is where our conversation about family must lead.
Not merely to stronger discipline.
Not merely to rearranged priorities.
Not merely to a better schedule with more prayer and fewer distractions.
It must lead to the cross.
Because the deepest problem in our hearts is not simply that we sometimes love good things too much.
It is that we are sinners who continually struggle to give the Creator the worship and obedience that belong to Him.
We exchange God's glory for created things.
We seek security in what cannot ultimately save us.
We build identities around blessings that were never meant to become our gods.
And even when we recognize what we have done, we cannot save ourselves by promising to try harder.
We need mercy.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Redeemer.
And that is exactly why Jesus came.
The Son of God entered our broken world, lived in perfect obedience, died for sinners, and rose again.
He bore our sins, not because we had finally learned to arrange our priorities correctly, but because grace reaches people who cannot make themselves righteous.
Romans 5:8 tells us:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became perfect parents.
Not after we repaired every family relationship.
Not after we stopped fearing rejection.
Not after we learned how to trust without trembling.
While we were still sinners.
That is the Gospel.
It speaks to the astonishing reality that Jesus receives repentant sinners, forgives their guilt, and transforms their lives by grace.
Maybe the scandal in your story is that you have spent years claiming to put God first while quietly living for everyone's approval.
Maybe it is that your home looks spiritually impressive from the outside, but your private life is filled with compromise.
Maybe you have used your children as an excuse to avoid obedience.
Maybe you have used ministry as an excuse to neglect your children.
Maybe you have wounded people in the name of protecting your family.
Or perhaps you have been wounded by someone who used “God first” to justify abandoning you.
Whatever your story, the answer is not to replace one form of bondage with another.
It is to come to Jesus.
With honesty.
With repentance.
With the broken pieces.
With the fears you are embarrassed to admit.
With the relationships you cannot fix through your own strength.
And to say:

“Lord Jesus, I have loved Your gifts without always honoring You as the Giver. Forgive me. Teach me to love my family in a way that reflects Your heart. Give me courage to obey You, humility to repent when I am wrong, and wisdom to recognize the difference between faithfulness and pride.”
That is not the prayer of someone who has everything figured out.
It is the prayer of someone who knows where grace is found.
And perhaps that is where your family begins to change.
Not when you become louder about religion.
Not when you start correcting everyone at the dinner table.
Not when you force your children to perform Christianity to protect your reputation.
But when they begin to see the fruit of Christ's work in you.
When you apologize without making excuses.
When you forgive without pretending evil is acceptable.
When you tell the truth without cruelty.
When you pray instead of manipulating.
When you refuse to sacrifice your convictions for approval.
When you serve your family faithfully, even when nobody notices.
When you show your children that following Jesus is not a performance for Sunday morning but a surrendered life that reaches into Monday's decisions.
Because a home centered on Christ is not a home without problems.
It is a home where problems are brought under the truth and grace of Christ.
And sometimes that transformation begins with one person.
One father who finally admits he has been spiritually absent.
One mother who stops measuring her worth by her children's achievements.
One husband who chooses integrity over appearances.
One wife who refuses to let fear govern her obedience.
One adult child who learns to honor parents while establishing biblically appropriate boundaries.
One believer who decides that keeping the peace is no longer an excuse for hiding the truth.
And one quiet prayer that changes the direction of a household.
There is something else we need to confront.
Some Christians hear a message about putting God first and immediately assume it means giving more money to a ministry.
Our salvation cannot be purchased.
And a ministry must never occupy the place of Christ.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That means Christian generosity should grow from grace, gratitude, conviction, and love—not guilt or spiritual pressure.
Yet voluntary support for faithful Gospel work can be a meaningful expression of stewardship.
Paul thanked the Philippian believers for their partnership in the Gospel in Philippians 1:5 and acknowledged their material support in Philippians 4:14–18.
Their generosity was not a payment for salvation.
It was a partnership in ministry.
If these messages have helped you return to Scripture, examine your heart, understand the Gospel, or find encouragement during a difficult season, you can help us continue and expand this work.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—a commitment of support that helps sustain the creation and sharing of Christ-centered teaching, encouragement, and discipleship resources.

It is not a replacement for your biblical responsibilities to your family or local church. Nor should it be treated automatically as a substitute for whatever convictions you hold concerning tithes and offerings.
It is simply an opportunity to participate in Gospel outreach through generous, willing support.
Not because spiritual growth can be bought.
But because we want to express appreciation to those who help sustain the work.
You are not less faithful.
You are not less loved by God.
You are not less welcome here.
The Gospel is not reserved for paying supporters.
We want people to have access to biblical nourishment whether or not they can financially contribute.
Because the purpose is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to keep pointing people toward Jesus.
And sometimes the simplest way to help that mission is something you can do right now.
Not merely to increase a number.
But because someone in your family, your church, or your circle of friends may be wrestling with this very question.
Someone may be trapped between love and fear.
Someone may be confusing family loyalty with obedience to God.
Someone may be using religious activity to escape responsibilities at home.
Someone may need to hear that putting Jesus first does not mean loving their family less, but learning to love them according to His truth.
And someone may be waiting for permission to stop pretending that everything is okay.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to accuse them.
But to open a door to Scripture, humility, and grace.
Because the day may come when you are standing in front of a difficult decision, caught between pleasing someone you deeply love and obeying what Christ has clearly commanded.
And on that day, you may need to remember that the approval of people is not the foundation of your identity.
Jesus is.
Not every person who encounters the Gospel will immediately agree.
But everyone deserves to hear the truth about Jesus Christ.
Not about someone else's family.
Not about that relative who keeps disappointing you.
Not about the Christian you think needs to read this.
About you.
Has there been a moment when you knew what Jesus wanted from you, but you were afraid of how your family would react?
Perhaps you stayed silent.
Perhaps you compromised.
Perhaps you obeyed, but it cost you dearly.
Perhaps you are still standing in the middle of that decision today.
And if you have experienced God's grace in a difficult family situation, consider sharing a brief testimony. Someone reading may need the encouragement that Christ has not abandoned them.
Because this is not about collecting perfect testimonies from perfect Christians.
It is about making room for honesty, prayer, repentance, and hope.
And I want to leave you with one final picture.
Imagine reaching the end of your life.
The house is quiet.
The children are grown.
The careers have ended.
The possessions you spent decades acquiring are no longer in your hands.
The approval you worked so hard to protect has faded.
And everything that once seemed so urgent has become strangely small.
What will matter then?
Not whether everyone always agreed with you.
Not whether you maintained a flawless family image.
Not whether you successfully avoided every uncomfortable conversation.
What will matter eternally is your relationship with Jesus Christ.
And what a precious legacy it would be if those who knew you best could say:

“They were not perfect. They made mistakes. They sometimes struggled with fear. But when they failed, they repented. When Scripture corrected them, they listened. When loving us was difficult, they did not stop loving us. And when following Jesus was costly, they kept turning toward Him.”
That is a legacy worth pursuing.
Not a family that worships itself.
Not a home that uses God as a decoration.
Not a religious performance designed to impress outsiders.
But a household learning, day by day, to live under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And perhaps today is the day to begin again.
To repent of whatever has taken His place.
To ask forgiveness from someone you have neglected.
To stop using family responsibilities as an excuse for disobedience.
To stop using religious commitments as an excuse for family neglect.
To love more faithfully.
To trust more deeply.
To surrender more completely.
Because Jesus is not asking you to choose between loving Him and loving your family well.
He is teaching you that only when He is Lord can you learn to love without turning love into an idol.
Your family is precious.
Your marriage matters.
Your children matter.
Your parents matter.
Your responsibilities matter.
But none of them can carry the weight of being your savior.
Only Jesus can do that.
And when He takes His rightful place, the goal is not a family pushed aside.
It is a family loved under the gracious lordship of Christ.
Do not give your family the impossible burden of being your god when the greatest gift you can give them is a life surrendered to Jesus.
